q: Which structure is found in a plant cell but not in an animal cell?
why: Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall; animal cells have only a cell membrane.

q: A cell is 20 µm long. In a drawing it is 40 mm long. What is the magnification?
why: 40 mm = 40 000 µm. Magnification = image ÷ actual = 40 000 ÷ 20 = ×2000.

q: What does mitosis produce?
why: Mitosis gives two cells with identical chromosomes to the parent, for growth and repair.

q: Where are stem cells found in plants?
why: Meristem tissue at root and shoot tips can differentiate into any plant cell type.

q: Which process moves substances against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration?
why: Active transport needs energy because it moves particles from low to high concentration.

q: A potato cylinder gets heavier in a sugar solution. What does this show?
c: The solution was more concentrated than the potato cells
Water moved into the potato by osmosis
why: Mass gain means water entered the cells by osmosis: the solution was more dilute than the cell sap.

q: Which list is in order from smallest to largest?
why: Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form organ systems.

q: What is a tissue?
c: A group of organs working together
A group of cells with a similar structure and function
why: A tissue is a group of similar cells working together, such as muscle tissue.

q: Which enzyme breaks down starch?
why: Amylase (a carbohydrase) breaks starch into sugars. Bile is not an enzyme.

q: Why are the walls of the left ventricle thicker than those of the right ventricle?
c: It pumps blood all around the body at high pressure
It receives blood from the lungs
why: The left ventricle pumps blood around the whole body, so it needs more muscle than the right, which only pumps to the lungs.

q: Which tissue transports water and mineral ions from the roots to the leaves?
why: Xylem carries water and minerals upwards; phloem carries dissolved sugars both ways.

q: Which condition increases the rate of transpiration?
why: Wind removes water vapour from around the leaf, keeping the concentration gradient steep.

q: Which disease is caused by a virus?
why: Measles is viral. Salmonella and gonorrhoea are bacterial; malaria is caused by a protist.

q: How do white blood cells defend the body?
c: By engulfing pathogens and producing antibodies and antitoxins
By making the blood clot only
why: White blood cells use phagocytosis, antibodies and antitoxins.

q: What is a monoclonal antibody?
c: An antibody made by many different lymphocytes
Identical antibodies from one clone of cells, targeting one specific antigen
why: Monoclonal antibodies come from a single clone (hybridoma) and bind to one specific antigen.

q: Which cells are fused to make a hybridoma?
c: A red blood cell and a tumour cell
A mouse lymphocyte and a tumour cell
why: The lymphocyte makes the antibody; the tumour cell makes the hybridoma divide repeatedly.

q: A plant has yellow leaves because of a lack of one mineral ion. Which ion?
why: Magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll; a deficiency causes chlorosis (yellow leaves).

q: Which is a physical defence of plants against pathogens?
why: The waxy cuticle is a physical barrier; antibacterial chemicals and poisons are chemical defences.

q: What is the word equation for photosynthesis?
why: Light energy is used to make glucose and oxygen from carbon dioxide and water.

q: At high light intensity, increasing the light further no longer raises the rate of photosynthesis. Why?
c: Another factor such as CO₂ concentration or temperature is now limiting
The enzymes are denatured by light
why: When light is no longer the factor in shortest supply, something else limits the rate.

q: What are the products of aerobic respiration?
why: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water, releasing energy.

q: Why does a sprinter breathe heavily after a race?
c: To repay the oxygen debt and break down lactic acid
why: Extra oxygen is needed to oxidise lactic acid built up during anaerobic respiration.

q: What is homeostasis?
c: Keeping internal conditions constant despite changes
why: Homeostasis is regulation of internal conditions such as blood glucose and temperature.

q: In a control system, what detects a change?
why: Receptors detect stimuli; coordination centres process; effectors respond.

q: Why are reflex actions fast?
c: They involve the conscious part of the brain
They do not involve the conscious part of the brain
why: Reflexes bypass conscious thought, so the response is automatic and rapid.

q: What happens at a synapse?
c: An electrical impulse jumps directly across
A chemical diffuses across the gap to the next neurone
why: Neurotransmitter chemicals diffuse across the synaptic gap and trigger an impulse in the next neurone.

q: Which hormone lowers blood glucose concentration?
why: Insulin from the pancreas makes cells take up glucose and the liver store it as glycogen.

q: Which gland produces adrenaline?
why: The adrenal glands release adrenaline, preparing the body for fight or flight.

q: Which plant hormone causes shoots to grow towards light?
why: Auxin gathers on the shaded side of a shoot and makes those cells elongate, bending it towards the light.

q: What is ethene used for commercially?
why: Ethene is used to ripen fruit during transport and storage.

q: A heterozygous tall plant (Tt) is crossed with a short plant (tt). What proportion of offspring are expected to be short?
why: Tt × tt gives Tt, Tt, tt, tt: half the offspring are tt (short).

q: How many chromosomes are in a human gamete?
why: Meiosis halves the chromosome number, so gametes have 23 chromosomes.

q: What is the original source of genetic variation?
why: New alleles arise by mutation; selection then acts on that variation.

q: Why are bacteria able to become resistant to antibiotics?
c: Antibiotics cause bacteria to adapt on purpose
A mutation gives some bacteria resistance, and they survive and reproduce
why: Resistant bacteria survive treatment and multiply, so the resistant strain spreads.

q: Why were Darwin's ideas only gradually accepted?
c: They challenged the idea that God made all organisms, and the mechanism of inheritance was unknown
why: Religious objections, limited evidence at the time and no known mechanism of inheritance slowed acceptance.

q: Which is evidence for evolution?
why: Fossils show how organisms have changed over millions of years.

q: Who proposed the three-domain system?
why: Carl Woese split organisms into Archaea, Bacteria and Eukaryota using chemical analysis.

q: Which part of a binomial name gives the genus?
c: Neither: it is the species only
why: In Homo sapiens, Homo is the genus and sapiens the species.

q: Which is an abiotic factor?
why: Abiotic factors are non-living: light, temperature, water, CO₂, soil pH.

q: What do plants compete with each other for?
c: Light, space, water and mineral ions
why: Plants compete for light, space, water and minerals; animals compete for food, mates and territory.

q: A quadrat of 0.25 m² contains 6 daisies on average. Estimate the number in a 100 m² field.
Which organisms return carbon to the atmosphere by decay?
c: Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi
why: Decomposers respire as they break down dead matter, releasing carbon dioxide.

q: Why does deforestation increase atmospheric carbon dioxide?
c: Trees release CO₂ when they grow
Less CO₂ is absorbed by photosynthesis, and burning or decay releases CO₂
why: Fewer trees remove CO₂, and burning or rotting wood adds more.

q: What does high biodiversity help an ecosystem do?
c: Be more stable and less dependent on any one species
why: Many species and interactions make an ecosystem more resilient to change.

q: Why is the biomass at each trophic level less than the level below?
c: Biomass is lost through respiration, waste and parts not eaten
why: Only around 10% passes on: the rest is used in respiration or lost in faeces, urine and uneaten parts.

q: Producers have 10 000 kJ of energy. About how much reaches the primary consumers?
why: Roughly 10% of energy is transferred between trophic levels.

q: What is mycoprotein made from?
why: Mycoprotein is grown from the fungus Fusarium in fermenters.

q: Why does keeping farm animals indoors in warm conditions increase efficiency?
c: Less energy is transferred to the surroundings and used for movement
why: Restricting movement and warmth means less energy is lost, so more becomes biomass.
